blocks.text: Muscle is the tissue that can contract in a coordinated way to produce movements of parts of the body or of the whole body. The individual cells of muscle are muscle fibres or myofibres. The ability of muscles to contract and relax not only lets the body move but also provides the force that pushes substances such as blood and food through the body.

blocks.title: Muscles in other animals
blocks.text: Essentially all animals employ muscles. When a mosquito flies, its wings are moved rapidly through the air by quickly contracting flight muscles; when an earthworm burrows through the soil, its movement is driven by strong muscles pushing its body past the surrounding soil.
Types of muscles
The human body has three types of muscle tissue: skeletal, smooth and cardiac.

items: Skeletal muscles move parts of the body such as the limbs, trunk and face. Their fibres are elongated cells with striations. Because their contractions are usually consciously controlled, skeletal muscles are voluntary muscles.

Smooth muscles are present in the walls of the stomach, intestines, blood vessels and other internal organs. Their fibres are spindle-shaped, have a single nucleus and lack striations, and are surrounded by connective tissue. Because most of their movements cannot be consciously controlled, smooth muscle is involuntary muscle.
Cardiac muscles are found only in the walls of the heart. Their fibres branch extensively and are striated like skeletal muscle, but each cell usually contains one nucleus near its centre.

blocks.text: Structure of skeletal muscles

The cells of skeletal muscle, the muscle fibres, are arranged in bundles enclosed by collagen fibres and connective tissue. At the ends of a muscle the collagen and connective tissue form tendons, which attach the muscle to bones.
Ultrastructure of skeletal muscles

Each skeletal muscle fibre is a cylindrical multinucleated cell enclosed by a plasma membrane, the sarcolemma. Its cytoplasm is the sarcoplasm and contains the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). The sarcolemma penetrates deep into the cell to form hollow elongated tubes, the transverse tubules (T-tubules), which reach the ends of the SR. Each fibre contains a bundle of 4 to 20 elongated thread-like myofibrils, made of two types of filament: thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin. The thick filaments create dark bands, the A-bands, and the thin filaments light bands, the I-bands; these alternating bands give skeletal muscle its striped (striated) appearance.

The thin actin filaments are attached to protein discs, the Z-lines. The section between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of muscle contraction. Within a sarcomere the thin filaments extend from the Z-line towards the centre, where they overlap with the thick filaments; this overlap creates the A-band, with a lighter central region, the H-band, where no overlap occurs. During contraction the thin filaments slide deeper into the A-band, so the H-band and I-band narrow and the A-bands are pulled closer together, shortening the muscle. The centre of the H-band may have a dark line, the M line, which helps to stabilise the thick filaments. In summary, a skeletal muscle is made of groups of cells, the muscle fibres; each fibre contains bundles of myofibrils in its cytoplasm; and each myofibril is made of two types of myofilament, myosin and actin.

blocks.text: Biochemistry of myofilaments

Thick myofilaments, about 16 nm in diameter, are made of many myosin proteins. Each myosin protein consists of two intertwined polypeptide chains ending in a globular head; these heads extend from the thick filament and connect to actin during contraction. Thin myofilaments, 7 to 8 nm in diameter, are made of three proteins: the core is two twisted strands of actin; two strands of tropomyosin wrap around the actin core and stiffen it, and in a relaxed fibre block the myosin-binding sites on the actin; and troponin, present at regular intervals, is made of three polypeptides, one inhibitory and binding to actin, a second binding tropomyosin to keep it in place, and a third binding calcium ions.

blocks.text: Mechanism of muscle contraction: the sliding filament model
The sliding filament model explains how a muscle contracts: the thin myofilaments slide past the thick ones so that they overlap to a greater degree. It occurs in the following steps.

blocks.alt: Two sarcomeres. Relaxed: actin filaments from the Z line at each end reach only part way in, leaving a wide H-zone around the middle of the myosin filaments, whose heads form cross-bridges. Contracted: the actin filaments have slid further over the myosin, the Z lines have moved closer (arrows) and the H-zone is narrow; the myosin filaments keep their length. Labels: Actin filaments, H-zone, Myosin filament, Z line, Cross-bridges.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.22: Sliding filament model of muscle contraction (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.22).

items: Sarcomeres at the relaxed state: in a relaxed muscle the sarcomeres are at their normal length. The myosin heads are not bound to actin because the binding sites on actin are blocked by the tropomyosin of the thin filaments; troponin is attached to the tropomyosin. The myosin heads have hydrolysed ATP into ADP and Pi.

Arrival of a nerve impulse: when a nerve impulse reaches the sarcolemma, the motor neuron releases a neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, at the synapse, which stimulates the sarcolemma to produce its own electrochemical impulses. These are carried into the fibre along the T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases calcium ions into the cytosol. The calcium ions bind to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.

Cross-bridges and the power stroke: when the binding sites are exposed, the myosin heads bind to them and form cross-bridges. The heads then release the ADP and Pi and undergo a conformational change, bending towards the centre of the sarcomere and pulling the actin filaments with them; this pulling action is the power stroke. It shortens the sarcomere, bringing the Z-lines closer together, and the H-zone disappears. It occurs simultaneously in all the sarcomeres, so the muscle contracts; the adjacent A-bands come closer to each other but do not shorten.

Separation of the myosin heads from actin: after pulling, the myosin head receives a new molecule of ATP, which lets it detach from actin. Splitting this ATP into ADP and Pi puts the head back into its original conformation, so the cross-bridge cycle can begin again.

blocks.alt: Four stages in a clockwise cycle joined by red arrows, each a thin filament above a thick filament with notes. Top: binding sites on actin are blocked; the myosin head holds ADP and P. Right: Ca ions bind with troponin, binding sites are open and the myosin head attaches (cross-bridge). Bottom: power stroke, the head releases ADP and P and pulls the actin filament towards the centre (arrows). Left: ATP attaches to the head, which detaches from actin.

blocks.title: Rigor mortis
blocks.text: After death the cells can no longer produce ATP, so the cross-bridges cannot be broken; this causes the muscle stiffness of death, rigor mortis. A living cell always has enough ATP to allow the myosin heads to detach from actin.
Arrangement of skeletal muscles at movable joints

Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough connective tissues, the tendons. Typically a muscle has two attachment points on different bones: the end attached to the bone that stays stationary during contraction is the origin, and the end attached to the bone that moves is the insertion; the middle part of the muscle is the belly. For the movement of bones at a joint in two directions, muscles work in pairs that produce opposing actions when they contract, an antagonistic arrangement. When one muscle, the flexor, contracts it bends the bone at the joint; when the opposing muscle, the extensor, contracts it straightens the bone. During such antagonistic action, when the flexor contracts the extensor is relaxed, and vice versa.

blocks.text: Movement at the knee joint

The knee joint is between the femur (thigh bone) and the tibia and fibula (lower leg bones). Flexion, or bending, of the lower leg is done by the hamstrings, a group of three muscles at the back of the thigh, which originate at the pelvic girdle and the top of the femur and insert on the upper parts of the fibula and tibia. Extension, or straightening, is done by the quadriceps, a group of four muscles at the front of the thigh, which originate at the ilium (part of the pelvic girdle) and femur and insert on the patella (kneecap) and tibia. When the hamstrings contract the lower leg bends and the quadriceps relax; when the quadriceps contract the lower leg straightens and the hamstrings relax.

blocks.alt: Two legs from the side. Left: the hamstrings at the back of the thigh contract and the lower leg is flexed (bent) backward; the relaxed quadriceps are not shown. Right: the quadriceps at the front of the thigh contract, pulling through the patella, and the lower leg is extended (straightened); the relaxed hamstrings are not shown.

blocks.title: Muscles pull, and the skeleton is a system of levers
blocks.text: Muscles can only pull, not push, because muscle fibres contract and shorten, pulling on tendons and so moving bones; when a muscle relaxes the bone moves back. To push, a muscle would have to be attached at both ends and draw both ends together, which is not possible. The skeleton works like a system of rods and levers: bones are the rods, giving structure and support and protecting the organs; joints are the fulcrums; muscles supply the effort; and the weight being moved is the load. When lifting a weight, the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps provides the effort and the weight is the load.
Muscle disorders

items: Muscle fatigue is a decline in muscle performance after prolonged or intense physical activity or because of disease; its symptoms are pain, decreased strength and reduced endurance. It arises because the ATP used for contraction is depleted so the muscle can no longer contract; because working muscles produce metabolic wastes such as lactate, hydrogen ions and reactive oxygen; because repeatedly activated fibres handle calcium ions less effectively; and because prolonged or intense exercise slightly damages the fibres, causing inflammation. It typically improves with rest, and severe fatigue needs medical attention.

Muscle cramps are sudden, involuntary and often painful contractions of a muscle or group of muscles, lasting from a few seconds to several minutes, most commonly in the legs and feet. Causes include dehydration, an imbalance of salts, overuse or injury of the muscle, certain medications such as diuretics, and conditions such as diabetes, liver disease and nerve damage. Gently stretching and massaging the muscle, applying heat or cold and pain-relieving medication relieve them.

Tetany is involuntary muscle contractions or spasms due to increased muscle tone and hyperexcitability of the nerves, in the hands, feet, face or larynx. Its most common cause is hypocalcaemia (a low level of calcium in the blood), which may be due to vitamin D deficiency, renal failure or thyroid disorders; it may also be due to other salt imbalances such as low magnesium. Treatment depends on the cause: for salt imbalances, calcium or magnesium supplements or intravenous fluids restore the electrolyte balance.
